conversation.content: Let's design a web search engine — something like Google. I know it's a massive system, so feel free to scope it how you see fit. What's your approach?

A search engine is a huge system, so rather than try to present the final architecture upfront, I'd like to build it incrementally — start with the simplest version that works and then layer on complexity. This mirrors how you'd actually build it in practice and lets us discuss trade-offs at each step. Can I start with a single-machine search engine and evolve from there?
I love that approach. Go ahead.

Layer 1: single-machine search. We have a corpus of documents. We build an inverted index — for each word, store a list of document IDs that contain it. When a query comes in, we look up each query term in the index, intersect the posting lists, and return matching documents. Storage: the index for 1 million web pages might be 5-10 GB — fits in memory on one machine. Serving: a single query takes microseconds for the index lookup. This handles maybe 10,000 QPS on one machine. It works. It just doesn't have enough documents or any ranking.
Good start. What's missing?

Three things: we need more documents (the web has billions of pages), we need ranking (not all matching documents are equally relevant), and we need a crawler to discover and fetch pages. Let me add ranking first since it transforms the search quality without changing the architecture. Layer 2: adding TF-IDF ranking. For each posting in the inverted index, we store not just the document ID but also the term frequency. At query time, we compute a TF-IDF score for each matching document — how often the term appears in this document weighted by how rare the term is across all documents. We sort results by score. This is still single-machine, still fast, but now results are meaningfully ranked.
How would you improve ranking beyond TF-IDF?

TF-IDF only uses the text content. The key insight of Google's original breakthrough was using link structure. Layer 2b: PageRank. Each page has a score based on how many other pages link to it, weighted by those pages' own importance. It's a recursive definition solved iteratively — initialize all pages with equal rank, then repeatedly propagate rank through the link graph until convergence. PageRank is computed offline as a batch job over the entire link graph. The score is stored alongside each document and used as a signal in the ranking function. Now we have: TF-IDF for query-document relevance plus PageRank for document authority. The final score is a weighted combination.
Good. Now we need more than one million pages. How do we scale the index?

Layer 3: distributing the index. We need to index billions of pages. Two sharding strategies for an inverted index: document-partitioned and term-partitioned. With document-partitioning, each shard holds the complete inverted index for a subset of documents. A query goes to every shard, each returns its top-K results, and a coordinator merges them. With term-partitioning, each shard holds the complete posting list for a subset of terms. A query only hits the shards that own the query terms. I'd go with document-partitioning. It's simpler — each shard is independent and self-contained. Term-partitioning creates hot spots (common terms have massive posting lists) and requires coordination between shards for multi-term queries.
With document-partitioning, every query hits every shard. How does that scale?

Good question. Let's say we have 10 billion pages. At 10KB per document's index entry, that's 100TB of index data. With 100 shards, each has 1TB — fits in memory with the right hardware. Each shard handles the query independently and returns its local top-50. The coordinator merges 100 lists of 50 — that's fast, just a priority queue merge. The bottleneck is the fan-out: 100 shard queries per user query. At 100K QPS from users, that's 10 million shard queries per second. Each shard sees 100K QPS — manageable with replication. If we replicate each shard 3x, each replica handles 33K QPS. That's well within what an in-memory index can handle.
Now let's talk about crawling. How do you discover and fetch web pages?

Layer 4: the crawler. It starts with a seed set of URLs — maybe a few thousand known sites. It fetches a page, extracts all the links from the HTML, and adds new URLs to a frontier queue. The crawler is inherently parallel — hundreds of machines each fetching pages concurrently. Key design constraints: politeness (don't hit the same domain too frequently — respect robots.txt and impose a per-domain rate limit of maybe 1 request per second), URL deduplication (the frontier grows fast — we need a bloom filter or a distributed set to avoid re-crawling the same URL), and prioritization (fresh content from important sites should be re-crawled more frequently than stale content from obscure sites).
How do you keep the index fresh? The web changes constantly.

Layer 5: freshness. The crawler needs to revisit pages. The question is how often. We can't re-crawl the entire web every day — that would require fetching 10 billion pages per day, about 115,000 pages per second. Instead, we prioritize: pages that change frequently (news sites, social media) get re-crawled hourly. Stable pages (Wikipedia articles, documentation) get re-crawled weekly or monthly. We estimate change frequency by tracking the diff between consecutive crawls. For freshness-sensitive queries (like searching for today's news), we can maintain a separate 'real-time' index that's smaller but updated within minutes. The main index is rebuilt periodically — say every few hours — from the latest crawl data.
Let's come back to query serving. How do you handle latency? Users expect results in under 200ms.

Layer 6: latency optimization. Several techniques. First, the index lives in memory — no disk I/O for the hot path. Second, for common queries, we cache the complete result page. The top 10,000 most common queries probably account for 30% of all traffic. Third, index compression — posting lists are sorted by document ID, so we can delta-encode and varint-compress them, reducing memory footprint and improving cache locality. Fourth, early termination — if we've already found 1,000 highly relevant results, we can stop scanning the remaining posting list entries. Fifth, geographic routing — serve queries from the nearest data center to minimize network RTT. The latency budget is roughly: 5ms network to data center, 50ms for shard queries in parallel, 10ms for merge and ranking, 5ms for serialization. Total ~70ms, well under 200ms.
What about the modern aspect — ML-based ranking? Where does that fit in your incremental model?

Layer 7: learning to rank. TF-IDF and PageRank are static signals. Modern search uses hundreds of features in an ML model: query-document textual similarity (BM25, which generalizes TF-IDF), click-through rate data (which results users actually click for this query), freshness, domain authority, page load speed, mobile-friendliness, and semantic understanding via embeddings. The ranking pipeline is multi-stage to manage cost: first, a cheap retrieval stage using the inverted index returns maybe 10,000 candidates. Then a lightweight ranker (like a gradient-boosted tree) scores and prunes to 500. Finally, an expensive neural model (like a BERT cross-encoder) re-ranks the top 500 to produce the final top 10. Each stage is more expensive but operates on fewer documents.
This incremental approach is excellent. How do you handle spam and abuse in the index?

Multiple layers of defense. At crawl time: detect and filter content farms, link farms, and keyword-stuffed pages using heuristics (unnatural keyword density, hidden text, cloaking — showing different content to the crawler than to users). At index time: demote pages with suspicious link profiles — if a page suddenly gets 10,000 links from newly created domains, that's a link scheme. At query time: the ranking model implicitly handles this — spam pages tend to have low click-through rates and high bounce rates, so the ML model learns to rank them low. We also have a manual review team for high-impact cases. It's an arms race — spammers adapt, so the system needs continuous updates.
Let's talk about failure handling. A shard goes down during a query — what happens?

Since each shard is replicated, the query coordinator routes to a replica instead. If all replicas of a shard are down — which is rare — we have a choice: return partial results (missing that shard's documents) or fail the query. I'd return partial results with slightly degraded quality. The user won't notice that 1% of the web is missing from results. The coordinator sets a timeout — if a shard doesn't respond within 30ms, skip it and merge the results from the responding shards. This is the same approach Google uses — they call it 'good enough' serving. Better to return slightly incomplete results fast than to make users wait for a slow shard.
We're running out of time. Can you summarize the layers you built?

Sure. Layer 1: single-machine inverted index for basic keyword search. Layer 2: TF-IDF and PageRank for ranking quality. Layer 3: document-partitioned sharding across 100+ nodes for scale. Layer 4: distributed web crawler with politeness and deduplication. Layer 5: freshness management with adaptive re-crawling and a real-time index for breaking content. Layer 6: latency optimization through caching, compression, early termination, and geographic distribution. Layer 7: multi-stage ML ranking for relevance quality. Each layer can be designed, built, and validated independently before adding the next. That's how I'd approach building this in practice — ship value early and iterate.
That was one of the best-structured system design answers I've heard. The incremental approach made a complex system feel approachable, and you maintained depth at every layer. Excellent interview.

strengths: Exceptional communication structure — incremental layered approach made a massive system tractable
Deep knowledge at every layer — inverted index internals, sharding strategies, crawling, ML ranking pipeline
Strong capacity estimation with realistic numbers at each layer
Practical failure handling with partial results and timeout-based degradation
weaknesses: Minimal requirements gathering — jumped straight to building without clarifying scale expectations
API design was never discussed — no search API specification, pagination, or query syntax
Didn't discuss indexing pipeline details — how documents flow from crawler to the searchable index
